text: Metadata gets into a catalog one of two ways, and a mature program uses both, deliberately. Automated scanning connects directly to source systems and pulls technical metadata automatically. Manual curation is a human adding the business layer scanning can never produce on its own.

A catalog built on scanning alone is technically comprehensive and completely useless for business users — it can tell you CustomerId is an INT, but not that it's the key every revenue report joins on. A catalog built on curation alone is accurate where someone bothered to write something, and silently empty everywhere else.
Scanning guarantees coverage. Curation supplies meaning. Neither substitutes for the other.

For dbo.Orders.OrderTotal, the scan captures DECIMAL, not null, row count, last modified — automatically, nightly. Curation adds the business definition, a glossary link, and an owner — written once by a steward, updated only when the meaning actually changes.

An organization that only scans gets meaningless entries. An organization that only curates gets silent gaps nobody notices. Running both is what makes a catalog genuinely trustworthy. Next lesson: metadata quality — the catalog has the same quality problem the data itself has.
